readerTitle: Why Zappos put its phone number on every page
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Zappos) + 전해지는 일화 (긴 통화) + 가상 적용 (사내 IT 헬프데스크)
insight: 고객 상담은 줄여야 할 비용이 아니라 고객이 회사를 기억하게 되는 마케팅 예산일 수 있다. 상담은 통화 비용이 아니라 그 통화가 만든 재구매와 입소문으로 판단한다.
misconception: 좋은 상담팀은 통화를 빨리 끝내고 건당 비용을 낮추는 팀이다. 상담 전화가 줄어들수록 좋다.

sources.text: Hsieh, T. (2010). Delivering Happiness: A Path to Profits, Passion, and Purpose. (서비스를 마케팅으로 본 관점, 라스베이거스 이전, 재구매·입소문 성장)
Zappos.com 반품 정책 페이지 (무료 배송·무료 반품, 365일 반품)
Taylor, B. (2008). Why Zappos Pays New Employees to Quit—And You Should Too. Harvard Business Review.
Frei, F., Ely, R., Winig, L. (2009). Zappos.com 2009: Clothing, Customer Service, and Company Culture. Harvard Business School case.
장시간 통화 일화에 대한 언론 보도 (2012년 이후 여러 매체)

factChecks.note: 무료 양방향 배송과 365일 반품 정책이 현재도 유효한지, 언제부터 시행됐는지 Zappos 공식 페이지로 확인하세요. 카드에는 시점 없이 정책만 적었습니다.
상담원에게 스크립트와 통화 시간 제한이 없었다는 점은 Hsieh(2010)와 HBS 사례에 나옵니다. 카드에는 '정해진 스크립트 없음, 통화 시간으로 평가하지 않음'으로만 적었습니다.
2004년 라스베이거스 이전 이유(상담 인력 채용)와 외주 대신 직접 운영하기로 한 결정은 Hsieh(2010) 기준입니다. 연도와 경위를 다시 확인하세요.
장시간 통화는 보도마다 시간이 다릅니다(약 10시간 이상). 카드에는 'reportedly more than ten hours'로만 적고 일화로 표시했습니다.
퇴사 보너스 금액은 시기마다 달랐습니다. 카드에는 금액을 적지 않았습니다. HBR(2008)로 확인하세요.
Amazon 인수: 2009년 발표, 종료 시점 주가 기준 약 $1.2B로 널리 보도됨(발표 시점 가치는 더 낮게 보도됨). 카드에는 'widely reported at about $1.2 billion'으로 적었습니다.
재구매 고객 비율 수치는 출처마다 달라 카드에 적지 않았습니다. '대부분 재구매와 입소문'이라는 표현이 Hsieh(2010) 내용과 맞는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why Zappos put its phone number on every page
body: Most online stores hide their phone number. Calls are expensive, so the goal is fewer of them.
Zappos, an online shoe store founded in 1999, did the opposite. It put its number at the top of its website and told staff to stay on the line as long as it took.

image.label: A website header with a big phone number
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 신발 쇼핑몰 웹사이트 상단에 전화번호가 크게 강조되어 있고, 옆에 헤드셋을 쓴 상담원이 웃으며 통화 중. 실제 Zappos 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: People won't buy shoes they can't try on.
body: It's the early 2000s. You sell shoes online. Customers worry about fit, so many hesitate. Your call center is growing and costs real money.
Where do you put your next dollar?

options.text: Cut call costs: short scripts, time targets, and a contact page that's hard to find
options.feedback: Your cost per call drops. But the nervous first-time buyer, the one you most need to win, now meets a rushed stranger.

options.text: Outsource the phones to a cheaper provider and spend the savings on ads
options.feedback: Ads bring people in, and costs fall. But the call is often the only human moment with your brand, and you've handed it to someone else.

options.text: Make returns free, run the phones yourself, and let staff take as long as needed
options.feedback: Expensive per call, but it removes the fear of buying and gives customers a story to tell. You treat service as part of marketing.

cards.title: It spent on the moment, not the ad.
body: Zappos chose a version of option C. According to Tony Hsieh, its longtime CEO, the company kept customer service in-house and moved to Las Vegas in 2004 partly to hire call-center staff.
The service rules looked costly:
list: **Free shipping both ways** and a 365-day return window
The phone number shown on every page
cards.callout: Each rule made it safer to try buying shoes online.
cards.softwareNote: The same choice shows up in software support. A team judged only on tickets closed per hour will close tickets fast. A team judged on whether customers stay and expand will solve the problem behind the ticket.

cards.title: Service as marketing
body: **Service as marketing** means treating a customer's contact with your staff as a chance to win future sales, not just a cost to cut.
Hsieh argued that money most companies spend on ads was better spent on service. A phone call is a **moment of truth**: a short contact that shapes how a customer feels about the whole company.
An ad is forgotten. A great call gets retold to friends.

image.label: Two paths: ad money vs service money
image.brief: 두 갈래 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Ad budget" 동전이 광고판으로 갔다가 흐려짐. 오른쪽 "Service budget" 동전이 상담 전화 → 만족한 고객 → 친구 여러 명에게 퍼지는 화살표로 이어짐.

cards.title: Generous service needs the right people.
body: No scripts only works if staff have good judgment. Zappos famously offered new hires a cash payment to quit after training. People who stayed for the job, not the money, were the ones it wanted.

The stories followed. In one widely reported anecdote, a single customer call lasted more than ten hours. Details vary between reports, but the point spread: this company won't rush you off the phone.
Stories like that cost a few hours of wages and travel further than most ads.

cards.title: Repeat customers did the selling.
body: Hsieh wrote that most of Zappos' growth came from repeat customers and word of mouth, not paid ads.
In 2009, Amazon bought Zappos in a deal widely reported at about **$1.2 billion**. Amazon already sold shoes. What it paid for was largely a loyal customer base and the culture behind it.
The cost per call was high. The value of what each call created was higher.

cards.title: This only pays if customers come back.
body: Free returns and long calls are real costs. They pay off when customers buy again and again and margins can absorb the returns.
A store that sells one-off items with thin margins may simply lose money copying Zappos.
And generosity without hiring and training is just chaos. Zappos built the culture first. Removing call-time targets from an untrained team won't create the same result.

cards.title: Now it's an internal IT help desk.
body: You lead the IT help desk in a 2,000-person company. Leadership wants lower cost per ticket. Employees complain that problems keep coming back after tickets are closed.
What do you change?

options.text: Set a 5-minute target per ticket to cut costs
options.feedback: Cost per ticket falls, but repeat tickets rise. Your colleagues lose hours, and trust in IT keeps dropping.

options.text: Judge the team on problems that stay fixed, and let staff take the time to solve root causes
options.feedback: Each ticket costs more, but fewer come back and colleagues start recommending IT. It's the Zappos logic inside a company.

options.text: Keep the targets but add a satisfaction survey after each ticket
options.feedback: You'll learn more about how people feel. But staff are still rewarded for speed, so behavior won't change much.

cards.title: Judge a service call by what it creates, not what it costs.
body: Zappos treated each call as marketing. That made expensive service a growth engine instead of a cost to shrink.
**Try it today:** pull up how your team measures customer contact. Ask whether any of those numbers reward ending the conversation sooner than the customer wants.
